transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Recording id: mf-20260519-nt-003
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Rivera (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (CTO, Novae), Jill Huang (Head of Infra), Kara Owens (Security), Tom Reyes (ML Eng), Liam Brooks (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
- Goal: scope a 4-week POC to validate Private networking + data residency requirements for Novaes therapeutic inference workloads.
- Key decisions: pilot to use AWS us-east-2 region, prefer PrivateLink if egress restrictions require strict no-internet paths; VPC peering acceptable if controlled egress and routing are fine.
- Benchmarks: target p50 < 90ms for short prompts (<=128 tokens), p95 < 250ms, sustained 20 qps at 4 concurrent workers for representative workload; cost/throughput tradeoff to be measured.
- Next actions: share security pack, confirm VPC ranges, schedule bench run.

Topics listed:
- Residency constraints and legal notes
- Connectivity options: VPC Peering vs PrivateLink vs Transit Gateway
- Egress policy and allow-listing
- Benchmark design and success criteria
- Pilot timeline and roll-in steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (AE, Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, we have Diego from the SE team who's going to run the bench and the network options with you, and Samir, do you want to kick off with your goals?
[00:12] Samir (CTO, Novae): Yeah thanks Maya. Real quick — we want to run a pilot to make sure inference stays inside our cloud boundary. We're regulated, so data residency and no egress to third-party datacenters is kinda mandatory. Also low latency for our clinician-facing UI is important.
[00:28] Jill (Head of Infra): And just to add, we have strict egress rules — only outbound to specific endpoints. We can't have callbacks to the public internet from the model infra.
[00:36] Maya: Got it, thanks. Diego — want to run through how Redwood supports private networking?
[00:42] Diego (SE): Sure. At a high level we support three patterns: VPC Peering, PrivateLink (VPC endpoint services), and Private Dedicated deployments inside customer VPCs for private control plane. For a pilot, the common choices are Peering or PrivateLink depending on your egress posture.
[00:57] [00:57] Tom (ML Eng): Quick question — does PrivateLink mean all traffic stays in our VPC and nothing traverses internet?
[01:03] Diego: In practice yes. PrivateLink provides an ENI in your VPC, so our service endpoints are reachable via AWS private networking and don't require NAT to go to public IPs. Peering can also be private, but with peering you can get more flexible routing but you might need to manage route tables carefully.
[01:20] Kara (Security): Are the logs and model artifacts stored on Redwood side or can they be disabled/retained only in our account? We need auditability and minimal retention by default.
[01:29] Maya: Good — our Private offering can be configured to keep logs in your VPC or forward only audit records to your SIEM. For hosted/Dedicated, we have retention controls and KMS integrations; I'll send SOC2 + KMS notes.
[01:40] [01:40] Samir: For the pilot we need to validate: 1) connectivity with no internet egress, 2) p95 latency under load, and 3) audit logs in our SIEM. That covers success criteria for legal & product.
[01:52] Diego: That maps well. For benchmarks, we generally measure per-model p50/p95 generation latency, tokens/sec throughput, and cost per 1k tokens. For your UI, what does a typical prompt look like?
[02:05] Tom: Most prompts are short — clinician notes and triage text, average 80 tokens, occasionally up to 300 tokens. Typical concurrency is 4 workers per region, peak QPS 18-25 across those workers.
[02:18] Diego: Great — we'll design the bench around that: a mix of 80-token and 250-token requests with concurrency ramps to 4 workers, sustained for 10 minutes per step. We'll collect p50/p95 and tokens/sec.
[02:30] Liam (PM): Is it realistic to expect consistent p95 under 300ms? Our UX team says 300ms is the upper bound for interactive flows.
[02:37] Diego: With cat model sizing and right quantization profile we typically hit p50 ~70-120ms and p95 under 300ms for <128 token responses on our Dedicated pools. Hosted tiers can be slightly more variable. We'll show tradeoffs on the bench.
[02:50] [02:50] Jill: On connectivity — if we choose peering, we have a default deny egress rule that only allows connection to our vendor endpoints; will Redwood require any public IPs for callbacks like model updates?
[03:02] Maya: For the pilot we can avoid callbacks. Updates and model pulls are on our side during a maintenance window — Diego will outline the bootstrap flow.
[03:10] Diego: Bootstrapping models requires fetching artifacts once; we can do that via a controlled egress path or pre-stage the model into a customer-managed S3 if you prefer zero egress during the pilot.
[03:21] Kara: Pre-staging is preferable. Also, can you support cross-account KMS so we can own encryption keys?
[03:28] Maya: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS keys for Private deployments; for hosted we can integrate with your KMS using grant flow. I'll attach the KMS implementation note.
[03:37] [03:37] Samir: About regions — we want compute to live in eu-west-2 primarily, but we also have a DR region in us-east-2. Can Redwood pin model serving to a specific region and avoid fallback to other regions?
[03:49] Diego: Yes, you can pin the model version to a region and set routing policies. For the pilot we'll keep everything in us-east-2 as you suggested earlier, unless you want eu-west-2. Pinning avoids automatic cross-region fallback.
[04:00] Tom: We might want to run a quick local benchmark inside eu-west-2 later; for now let’s do the pilot in us-east-2 to use Redwood's lowest-latency infra.
[04:08] Maya: Timeline idea: week 0 — prep and network config exchange; week 1 — base bench and smoke tests; week 2 — scale runs and failure modes; week 3 — polish and security review; closeout with results and decision. Any concerns?
[04:20] Jill: That seems reasonable. We need a strict network cutover window for the model bootstrap. Also our infra team will need clear IP ranges to allowlist.
[04:29] Diego: We'll provide the endpoint IP ranges and the PrivateLink ENI details. Note PrivateLink also lets you avoid wide allowlist by exposing only a service name and ENIs.
[04:40] [04:40] Kara: Regarding auditability — does Redwood provide immutable request/response logs or can those be scrubbed for PHI?
[04:47] Maya: We can redact PII and optionally not persist full user inputs. For compliance we can stream audit events to your SIEM and not persist transcript logs in Redwood. We'll document configurations.
[04:58] Tom: For the bench harness, what metrics do you capture? Are you able to measure KV cache hit rates and effective latency when the model uses long-context?
[05:06] Diego: Yes we capture token generation times, KV cache behavior, CPU/GPU utilization, and memory. For long context we emulate full KV sequences to measure perf regression. We'll include that in the bench plan.
[05:18] Liam: About success criteria — Samir mentioned three items. Can we make them numeric? I propose: 1) No internet egress during inference (binary), 2) p95 < 250ms for 80-token responses under 4 concurrent workers sustained, 3) audit events forwarded with under 30s lag.
[05:33] Samir: That looks good. Add cost guardrails: cost per 1k tokens not exceed our pilot estimate by more than 30% — otherwise we won't proceed.
[05:41] Diego: We'll include rough cost telemetry in the bench run and show delta vs open-source quantized options.
[05:48] [05:48] Jill: A technical nit — if we use peering, how do you handle DNS? Do you support private DNS names in our zone?
[05:56] Diego: We support both DNS options. For PrivateLink we can expose an AWS private DNS name, for peering you can resolve route via your route tables; we have docs with example zone configurations.
[06:08] Kara: I want to raise one more item: penetration testing and vulnerability scans. We'll need Redwood's external scan reports and scope for an on-site vulnerability assessment.
[06:16] Maya: We have a standard security pack that includes our last external pentest summary, SOC2 Type II report, and vulnerability disclosure process. I'll send that. For on-site or customer-lab scans we'll coordinate a time window.
[06:28] Tom: Great. On the bench payload — can Redwood simulate the mix of short and medium prompts plus occasional 300-token long completions? Also we have reranking flows where we send multiple candidates — would you include batching tests?
[06:40] Diego: Absolutely. We'll create a mixed workload: 60% short (80 tokens), 30% medium (200-300 tokens), 10% long; and a rerank path with 5-way candidate scoring to measure aggregate latencies. We'll also test batching scenarios and continuous KV cache reuse.
[06:55] Liam: Do you provide a test harness or should we run our own JMeter-style harness?
[07:02] Diego: We have a bench harness (scripted in golang/python) we can run from within your VPC or from Redwood test agents inside the same region depending on connectivity choice. For strict no-egress, we'd run the harness from your VPC against the PrivateLink endpoint.
[07:14] Maya: We'll attach the harness repo and a runbook. Diego, can you note required permissions for the harness?
[07:20] Diego: Yes — we need ability to create endpoint connections (for PrivateLink) or accept peering requests, and to open specific subnets for the ENI. We'll enumerate minimum IAM and route table changes in the checklist.
[07:33] [07:33] Samir: On the question of fallback — in case of capacity pressure, do you automatically reroute to a compatible model in another region? We need predictable behavior; auto-fallback could cause residency violations.
[07:44] Diego: By default we have smart routing and fallbacks, but for Private deployments we can disable cross-region fallback. We'll set strict routing policies for the pilot to prevent any cross-region failover.
[07:55] Jill: That gives us comfort. One more: how do you measure true egress — if some telemetry is sent to Redwood for metrics collection does that cross the boundary? We need metrics to stay inside our monitoring stack.
[08:06] Maya: For the pilot we'll forward metrics to your CloudWatch/Datadog via forwarders; Redwood will not ingest raw payloads. We'll provide a metrics forwarder and a toggle to send only aggregated metrics to Redwood services.
[08:18] Kara: Ok. Anything else on compliance?
[08:21] [08:21] Maya: I'll circle back with the SOC2 pack and the KMS notes. Also, Diego will propose a bench plan with scripts and expected duration.
[08:29] Diego: Bench plan outline: 1) Smoke 10 minutes, 2) Ramp to 4 concurrency for 30 minutes with mixed traffic, 3) Stress 60 minutes to measure scale and failure behavior, 4) Rerank and batching microbench. We'll provide the exact scripts.
[08:43] Tom: Sounds good. For timing — can we run the bench first week of June? Our infra changes will be ready by 2026-05-31.
[08:51] Maya: Yes — target bench week of 2026-06-01. We'll schedule SE time and confirm.
[08:57] Liam: Final quick ask — can Redwood provide a minimal cost estimate for Dedicated vs hosted for the pilot? We just need ballpark to compare the 30% guardrail.
[09:05] Diego: We'll include pilot cost ranges: hosted (pay-as-you-go) vs dedicated reserved hourly estimate; we'll send that in the follow-up.
[09:13] Maya: Ok, let's recap actions and owners.
[09:15] [09:15] Recap: Maya to send security pack + privatelink vs peering doc (due 2026-05-22). Diego to prepare bench harness and scripts (due 2026-05-29). Jill to provide VPC cidr and allowlist (due 2026-05-21). Tom to share sample prompts and SLOs (due 2026-05-25).
[09:36] Samir: Thanks — this is a good plan. We'll review the pack and push infra changes this week.
[09:41] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites for bench windows.
[09:46] End of call.
